oggetti/corona-australe/cosa: A small arc-shaped constellation, a semicircle of little stars. It lies below Sagittarius.
oggetti/corona-australe/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9 pm.
oggetti/corona-australe/dove: From Italy it is always very low, skimming the southern horizon, below the 'Teapot' of Sagittarius. From the southern hemisphere it passes high, almost overhead.
oggetti/corona-australe/come: With the naked eye under a dark sky and with a clear southern horizon; the arc of stars is pretty through binoculars, but there are no bright objects.
oggetti/corona-australe/origine: Corona Australis is Latin for 'southern crown'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/corona-australe/storia: For the Greeks it was a crown or a wreath of leaves at the feet of Sagittarius. It has no single, clear myth like its 'sister', Corona Borealis.
oggetti/corona-australe/stelle/0/signifi: An orange giant, the brightest star in the constellation.
oggetti/corona-australe/stelle/1/signifi: From the Latin for 'the southern one'. It is a white star.
oggetti/corona-australe/stelle/2/signifi: Through a small telescope it is a double star, two similar yellow stars.
oggetti/corona-boreale/cosa: A small and very pretty constellation: seven stars form a semicircle, like a crown. It lies between Arcturus and Vega.
oggetti/corona-boreale/quando: Evenings from May to July, highest in June at around 9 pm.
oggetti/corona-boreale/dove: From Italy it is very high, almost overhead, to the left of Arcturus. From the southern hemisphere it is low in the north.
oggetti/corona-boreale/come: With the naked eye; it has no bright objects, but it is home to T Coronae Borealis, a 'recurrent nova' that normally cannot be seen and that erupted in 1866 and 1946.
oggetti/corona-boreale/origine: Corona Borealis is Latin for 'northern crown'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/corona-boreale/storia: It is the crown of Ariadne, the princess of Crete who helped Theseus escape from the Minotaur's labyrinth. The god Dionysus, who married her, threw her wedding crown up into the sky.
oggetti/corona-boreale/stelle/0/signific: From the Arabic for 'the broken one', because the ring of the crown is not closed. It is also called Gemma, the jewel of the crown.
oggetti/corona-boreale/stelle/1/signific: From the Arabic for 'the two rows' (of stars). It is a white star.
oggetti/corona-boreale/stelle/2/signific: A white star, close to Alphecca.
oggetti/corvo/cosa: A small, easy constellation: four stars form a quadrilateral, like a sail. It lies below Virgo.
oggetti/corvo/quando: Evenings from April to June, highest in May at around 9 pm.
oggetti/corvo/dove: From Italy it is low in the south, to the right of Spica, the bright star of Virgo. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky.
oggetti/corvo/come: With the naked eye, even under a less than perfect sky; with a telescope you can find the Antennae Galaxies, two galaxies that are colliding.
oggetti/corvo/origine: Corvus is Latin for 'crow'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/corvo/storia: Apollo sent the crow to fetch water in a cup, but the bird stopped to eat figs. It came back late with a snake and lied, saying it was the snake's fault. Apollo put the crow, the cup (Crater) and the snake (Hydra) in the sky, and the crow can never drink.
oggetti/corvo/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the wing'. It is the brightest star in Corvus.
oggetti/corvo/stelle/1/significato: A yellow giant in the bottom corner of the quadrilateral.
oggetti/corvo/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the crow'. Through a small telescope it is a double star.
oggetti/corvo/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the beak'. It is an orange giant.
oggetti/coppa/cosa: A small, faint constellation shaped like a cup or goblet. It lies next to Corvus, above the body of Hydra.
oggetti/coppa/quando: Evenings from March to May, highest in April at around 9 pm.
oggetti/coppa/dove: From Italy it is low in the south, to the right of Corvus and below Leo. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky.
oggetti/coppa/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; it has no easy objects for binoculars.
oggetti/coppa/origine: Crater is Latin (from Greek) for 'cup', the bowl used for mixing wine. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/coppa/storia: It is Apollo's cup, in the same story as Corvus: the crow was supposed to fill it with water but stopped to eat figs. As a punishment the cup is in the sky not far away, but the crow can never reach it.
oggetti/coppa/stelle/0/significato: From the Latin for 'the lip', the rim of the cup. It is an orange giant, the brightest star.
oggetti/coppa/stelle/1/significato: A white star; a telescope shows a faint companion.
oggetti/coppa/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic 'al-ka's', 'the cup'. It is an orange giant at the base of the goblet.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/cosa: The smallest constellation of all, but one of the most famous: four bright stars form a cross in the southern Milky Way.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from April to June, highest in May at around 9 pm.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the south; if you extend the long arm of the cross about four and a half times, you reach the south pole of the sky. Next to it are Alpha and Beta Centauri, 'the Pointers'.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/come: With the naked eye; with binoculars, next to Mimosa, you can find the 'Jewel Box' (NGC 4755), a cluster of colourful stars, and nearby is the dark cloud of the Coalsack.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/origine: Crux is Latin for 'cross'. Its stars were known to the Greeks as part of Centaurus; it became a constellation in its own right at the end of the 16th century, thanks to European navigators and cartographers.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/storia: For navigators heading south it was the landmark for finding the south celestial pole, where there is no pole star. Today it appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand and Brazil.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/stelle/0/significa: The name comes from 'Alpha Crucis'. It is the brightest star, at the foot of the cross; through a telescope it is double.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/stelle/1/significa: A very hot blue star, on the left arm of the cross.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/stelle/2/significa: The name comes from 'Gamma Crucis'. It is a red giant at the top of the cross: you can see its orange colour.
oggetti/croce-del-sud/stelle/3/significa: The faintest of the four main stars of the cross. It is a blue-white star.
oggetti/delfino/cosa: A small constellation shaped like a kite or a leaping dolphin: a diamond of four stars with a short tail.
oggetti/delfino/quando: Evenings from August to October, highest in September at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/delfino/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, a little north-east of Altair, the brightest star in Aquila. From the southern hemisphere it can be seen in the north, halfway up the sky.
oggetti/delfino/come: You can see it with the naked eye from a not too light-polluted sky, and it is pretty through binoculars; through a small telescope γ Del is a lovely double star.
oggetti/delfino/origine: Delphinus is Latin for 'dolphin'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/delfino/storia: In Greek myth it is the dolphin that persuaded the Nereid Amphitrite to marry Poseidon, who put it in the sky out of gratitude. Another story links it to the poet Arion, saved by a dolphin after being thrown into the sea. In English the diamond of stars is called 'Job's Coffin'.
oggetti/delfino/stelle/0/significato: Read backwards it is 'Venator', the Latinised surname of Niccolò Cacciatore, an astronomer at the Palermo Observatory: the name appeared in the Palermo catalogue of 1814.
oggetti/delfino/stelle/1/significato: Read backwards it is 'Nicolaus', the first name of Niccolò Cacciatore: his joke was only understood years later.
oggetti/delfino/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the dolphin'. It marks the dolphin's tail.
oggetti/delfino/stelle/3/significato: It is part of γ Delphini, a double star much loved by telescope observers.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/cosa: A southern constellation of faint stars, shaped like a long fish. It contains most of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a galaxy close to our own.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from December to February, highest in January at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it is high in the south, not far from Canopus: the easiest landmark is the Large Magellanic Cloud, a pale patch that looks like a piece broken off the Milky Way.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/come: The Large Magellanic Cloud is easy to see with the naked eye; with binoculars, look inside it for the Tarantula Nebula (NGC 2070).
oggetti/pesce-dorato/origine: Dorado is the Spanish and Portuguese name for the mahi-mahi (dolphinfish), a fish with golden glints. It was introduced by Plancius at the end of the 16th century, based on the observations of the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/storia: The Dutch navigators sailing to the East Indies often saw these fish alongside their ships and put one in the sky. In 1987 the supernova SN 1987A exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, the first visible to the naked eye since 1604.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/stelle/0/significat: The brightest star in the constellation, blue-white; even so, it is fairly modest.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/stelle/1/significat: A Cepheid variable: its light rises and falls over a cycle of about 10 days, and the change can be noticed even with the naked eye.
oggetti/pesce-dorato/stelle/2/significat: It gave its name to a family of gently pulsating stars, the 'Gamma Doradus' variables.
oggetti/dragone/cosa: A long serpent of stars winding between Ursa Major and Ursa Minor. The head is a small quadrilateral of four stars, near Vega.
oggetti/dragone/quando: Being very far north, it can be seen almost all year round; the best evenings are from June to August, highest in July at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/dragone/dove: From Italy it is high in the north, and in summer the head passes almost directly over the observer's head, a little north-west of Vega; the tail runs between the two Bears. It cannot be seen from the southern hemisphere.
oggetti/dragone/come: With the naked eye to follow its shape, preferably under a dark sky; the Cat's Eye Nebula (NGC 6543) is also here, but you need a telescope to see it.
oggetti/dragone/origine: Draco is Latin for 'dragon'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/dragone/storia: In Greek myth it is Ladon, the dragon that guarded the golden apples in the garden of the Hesperides and was killed by Hercules: indeed, in the sky Hercules has one foot on Draco's head. A curious fact: almost 5,000 years ago, at the time of the pyramids, the pole star was Thuban (α Dra), not today's Polaris.
oggetti/dragone/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'al-tinnin', 'the serpent' or 'the dragon'. It is an orange giant, the brightest star in Draco, in the head.
oggetti/dragone/stelle/1/significato: A yellow giant in Draco's body, towards Ursa Minor.
oggetti/dragone/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the serpent's head': with Eltanin it forms the dragon's two 'eyes'.
oggetti/cavallo/cosa: Very small: it is the second-smallest constellation in the sky, after the Southern Cross. A little trapezium of faint stars next to Delphinus.
oggetti/cavallo/quando: Evenings from August to October, highest in September at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/cavallo/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, between Delphinus and the head of Pegasus. From the southern hemisphere it can be seen in the north, halfway up the sky.
oggetti/cavallo/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns, and it has no notable objects for binoculars.
oggetti/cavallo/origine: Equuleus is Latin for 'foal', 'little horse'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/cavallo/storia: It has no particular myth: it represents just the head of a horse, close to the larger head of Pegasus. Some scholars think it was introduced by Hipparchus in the 2nd century BC, but this is not certain.
oggetti/cavallo/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'qit'at al-faras', 'piece of the horse': indeed, the figure is just a horse's head.
oggetti/cavallo/stelle/1/significato: It is really two stars very close together, orbiting each other; to the naked eye and through binoculars they look like one.
oggetti/eridano/cosa: The river of the sky: a very long line of stars that winds from Orion's foot down to the southern sky. It is one of the largest constellations.
oggetti/eridano/quando: Evenings from November to January, highest in December at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/eridano/dove: From Italy only the northern part can be seen, low in the south, starting next to Rigel, Orion's foot; from Sicily and southern Italy you can see a bit more of it, skimming the horizon, but the river mouth with Achernar always stays hidden. From the southern hemisphere you can see all of it, high in the sky.
oggetti/eridano/come: With the naked eye, with patience, because nearly all its stars are modest; look for ε Eridani, a star similar to the Sun about 10.5 light years away, visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/eridano/origine: Eridanus is the name of a mythical river, which Latin writers identified with the Po. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD): for him the river ended at Acamar, and the stretch down to Achernar was added later.
oggetti/eridano/storia: In myth Phaethon, son of the Sun, lost control of the Sun's chariot and was struck down by a thunderbolt from Zeus: he fell into the river Eridanus. For the Latin poets that river was the Po, and Phaethon's sisters, weeping for him on its banks, turned into poplar trees.
oggetti/eridano/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'akhir an-nahr', 'the end of the river'. It is one of the brightest stars in the sky and spins so fast that it is flattened; it can never be seen from Italy.
oggetti/eridano/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the chair' or 'the footstool': with nearby stars it was the footstool at Orion's feet. It lies next to Rigel.
oggetti/eridano/stelle/2/significato: Same meaning as Achernar, 'the end of the river': in Ptolemy's time the river ended here. From Italy it skims the southern horizon.
oggetti/eridano/stelle/3/significato: From the Arabic for 'the boat'. It is a red giant.
oggetti/fornace/cosa: A small southern constellation of faint stars, tucked into the bend of the river Eridanus.
oggetti/fornace/quando: Evenings from November to January, highest in December at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/fornace/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon, below Cetus and inside the bend of Eridanus. From the southern hemisphere it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/fornace/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; there is little to see with the naked eye or binoculars.
oggetti/fornace/origine: Fornax is Latin for 'furnace'. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 under the name Fornax Chemica, 'the chemical furnace', the kind used in laboratories.
oggetti/fornace/storia: Lacaille observed the southern sky from the Cape of Good Hope and filled the empty spaces with instruments of the science and arts of his day. In this part of the sky the Hubble Space Telescope took the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, one of the deepest images of the universe, full of extremely distant galaxies.
oggetti/fornace/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the ostrich': the name originally belonged to other stars in the area. A telescope shows that it has a companion.
oggetti/fornace/stelle/1/significato: Second in brightness, yet only magnitude 4.5: you need a dark sky to see it.
oggetti/gemelli/cosa: Two almost parallel lines of stars starting from two bright stars close together, Castor and Pollux: they are the heads of the two twins.
oggetti/gemelli/quando: Evenings from January to March, highest in February at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/gemelli/dove: From Italy it is high in the south, north-east of Orion: if you extend the line from Rigel to Betelgeuse you arrive near Castor and Pollux. From the southern hemisphere it is seen low in the north, upside down.
oggetti/gemelli/come: With the naked eye; with binoculars, look for the open cluster M35, near the twins' feet.
oggetti/gemelli/origine: Gemini is Latin for 'twins'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD) and is part of the zodiac.
oggetti/gemelli/storia: They are the Dioscuri, Castor and Pollux, brothers of Helen: when Castor died, Pollux, who was immortal, asked Zeus to let him share his immortality with him, and so they stay together in the sky. Ancient sailors considered them protectors of seafarers. In mid-December the Geminids, one of the richest meteor showers of the year, seem to come from here.
oggetti/gemelli/stelle/0/significato: From the Latin Pollux, the boxer twin. It is an orange giant about 34 light years away, brighter than Castor even though it carries the letter Beta.
oggetti/gemelli/stelle/1/significato: Named after the twin Castor, the tamer of horses. It looks like a single star, but it is a system of six stars.
oggetti/gemelli/stelle/2/significato: A name of Arabic origin. A white star marking Pollux's foot.
oggetti/gemelli/stelle/3/significato: A red giant whose light varies slightly, at the feet of the Twins.
oggetti/gru/cosa: A southern constellation shaped like a long-necked bird: a curved line of stars with two bright stars, Alnair and Tiaki.
oggetti/gru/quando: Evenings from September to November, highest in October at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/gru/dove: From central Italy only its northern part can be seen, skimming the southern horizon, below Fomalhaut; from Sicily and southern Italy Alnair and Tiaki also appear, very low. From the southern hemisphere it is high, almost overhead.
oggetti/gru/come: With the naked eye; δ Gruis is a pair of stars that can already be split with the naked eye or binoculars.
oggetti/gru/origine: Grus is Latin for 'crane'. It was introduced by Plancius at the end of the 16th century, based on the observations of the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman.
oggetti/gru/storia: Arab astronomers considered these stars part of the tail of Piscis Austrinus, the Southern Fish, which is why Alnair and Aldhanab have names linked to a tail. The Dutch navigators turned them into a bird instead.
oggetti/gru/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the bright one' (of the fish's tail). A blue-white star.
oggetti/gru/stelle/1/significato: A Polynesian name adopted by the IAU. It is a red giant: with the naked eye you can see that its colour differs from Alnair's.
oggetti/gru/stelle/2/significato: From the Arabic for 'the tail' (of the fish).
oggetti/ercole/cosa: Large, but with stars that are not bright. Its centre is the 'Keystone', four stars in the shape of a trapezium between Vega and Arcturus.
oggetti/ercole/quando: Evenings from June to August, highest in July at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/ercole/dove: From Italy it is very high, almost overhead, between Vega and Corona Borealis. From the southern hemisphere it is seen low in the north, upside down.
oggetti/ercole/come: With binoculars, look for M13, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, on the western side of the Keystone: a small smudge of light made of hundreds of thousands of stars.
oggetti/ercole/origine: Hercules is the Latin name of the Greek hero Heracles. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD), although he called it 'the kneeling man'.
oggetti/ercole/storia: The earliest Greeks saw a nameless kneeling man; only later was he identified with Heracles, the hero of the twelve labours. In the sky he is upside down, with one foot on Draco's head. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope sent a radio message towards M13.
oggetti/ercole/stelle/0/significato: From the Greek for 'club bearer', the club being Hercules' weapon. It is a yellow giant.
oggetti/ercole/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic 'ra's al-jathi', 'the head of the kneeling one'. A red giant whose light varies, with a companion visible through a telescope.
oggetti/ercole/stelle/2/significato: One of the corners of the Keystone. It is a system of two stars very close together.
oggetti/orologio/cosa: A southern constellation of faint stars: a long, irregular line next to the river Eridanus.
oggetti/orologio/quando: Evenings from November to January, highest in December at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/orologio/dove: From central Italy only the far northern end can be seen, with α Hor, skimming the southern horizon; from Sicily and southern Italy you can see a bit more of it, still skimming the horizon. From the southern hemisphere it is high in the south, not far from Achernar.
oggetti/orologio/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; it has no easy objects for binoculars.
oggetti/orologio/origine: Horologium is Latin for 'clock'. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 as Horologium Oscillatorium, 'the pendulum clock'.
oggetti/orologio/storia: Lacaille filled the southern sky with scientific instruments; here he wanted to commemorate the pendulum clock, invented by Christiaan Huygens in the 17th century and essential for measuring time precisely during astronomical observations.
oggetti/orologio/stelle/0/significato: An orange giant, the only even slightly noticeable star in the constellation.
oggetti/orologio/stelle/1/significato: Second in brightness, but already faint: you need a dark sky.
oggetti/idra/cosa: The largest constellation in the sky: a very long water snake. The head is a small group of stars below Cancer, then the body runs south-east until it is below Virgo.
oggetti/idra/quando: Evenings from February to April, highest in March at around 9-10 pm; the tail is best seen in May.
oggetti/idra/dove: From Italy the head is halfway up the sky towards the south, and the rest is low on the southern horizon; Alphard is the only bright star in an empty area, below and to the right of Regulus. From the southern hemisphere it is high in the sky.
oggetti/idra/come: With the naked eye to follow the snake; with binoculars, look for the open cluster M48, near the border with Monoceros.
oggetti/idra/origine: Hydra means 'water snake'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/idra/storia: It is linked to the Lernaean Hydra, the many-headed monster killed by Hercules. Another myth tells that Apollo sent a crow to fetch water in a cup; the crow was late and blamed a snake, and Apollo put all three in the sky: Hydra, Corvus and Crater, which indeed sit on the snake's back.
oggetti/idra/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'al-fard', 'the solitary one': it is the only bright star in an empty area. An orange giant.
oggetti/idra/stelle/1/significato: A yellow giant towards the tail, below Virgo.
oggetti/idra/stelle/2/significato: Part of the small group of stars that forms the snake's head.
oggetti/idra-maschio/cosa: A southern constellation near the south celestial pole: a large triangle of three stars between the two Magellanic Clouds and Achernar.
oggetti/idra-maschio/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere at 34° south it never sets, and the best evenings are from November to January, highest in December at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/idra-maschio/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it is high in the south, between the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.
oggetti/idra-maschio/come: With the naked eye for the three main stars; it has no easy objects, but next to it is the Small Magellanic Cloud, which belongs to Tucana.
oggetti/idra-maschio/origine: Hydrus means 'male water snake', to distinguish it from Hydra. It was introduced by Plancius at the end of the 16th century, based on the observations of the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman.
oggetti/idra-maschio/storia: It is one of the twelve constellations that came from the Dutch voyages to the East Indies. Johann Bayer made them famous by publishing them in his atlas Uranometria in 1603.
oggetti/idra-maschio/stelle/0/significat: A star similar to the Sun, a little older, about 24 light years away: one of the closest of those visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/idra-maschio/stelle/1/significat: It lies near Achernar and marks the snake's head.
oggetti/idra-maschio/stelle/2/significat: A red giant at the other corner of the triangle.
oggetti/indiano/cosa: An inconspicuous southern constellation: a small triangle of faint stars between Grus and Pavo.
oggetti/indiano/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from August to October, highest in September at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/indiano/dove: From central Italy it never rises; from Sicily and southern Italy you can glimpse part of it, with α Indi, skimming the horizon. From the southern hemisphere it is high in the south, almost overhead.
oggetti/indiano/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky; it contains ε Indi, a star similar to the Sun about 12 light years away, visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/indiano/origine: Indus is Latin for 'the Indian'. It was introduced by Plancius at the end of the 16th century, based on the observations of the Dutch navigators Keyser and de Houtman.
oggetti/indiano/storia: It represents a native person, perhaps from one of the peoples the Dutch navigators met on their voyages: nobody knows for sure which.
oggetti/indiano/stelle/0/significato: It comes from the star's Chinese name, which means 'Persia'. It is an orange giant.
oggetti/indiano/stelle/1/significato: Second in brightness, orange in colour.
oggetti/lucertola/cosa: A small zigzag constellation between Cygnus and Cassiopeia: a line of faint stars.
oggetti/lucertola/quando: Evenings from September to November, highest in October at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/lucertola/dove: From Italy it passes almost overhead, between Deneb and Cassiopeia. From the southern hemisphere only part of it can be seen, very low in the north.
oggetti/lucertola/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; the Milky Way crossing its northern part is beautiful through binoculars.
oggetti/lucertola/origine: Lacerta is Latin for 'lizard'. It was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in 1687.
oggetti/lucertola/storia: Hevelius filled small empty areas between the ancient constellations with new figures. This is where you find BL Lacertae, which looked like a variable star but is actually the extremely active core of a distant galaxy: it gave its name to a class of objects, the 'BL Lacs'.
oggetti/lucertola/stelle/0/significato: A white star, the brightest, in the northern part of the constellation.
oggetti/lucertola/stelle/1/significato: It lies at the southern end of the zigzag.
oggetti/leone-minore/cosa: A small constellation of faint stars between Leo and Ursa Major, with no obvious shape.
oggetti/leone-minore/quando: Evenings from March to May, highest in April at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/leone-minore/dove: From Italy it is high, almost overhead, between the head of Leo and the paws of Ursa Major. From the southern hemisphere it is seen low in the north.
oggetti/leone-minore/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; it has no easy objects.
oggetti/leone-minore/origine: Leo Minor is Latin for 'lesser lion'. It was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in 1687.
oggetti/leone-minore/storia: Hevelius created it from stars that did not belong to any figure, below Ursa Major: it has no myths. A curious fact: it has a Beta star but no Alpha, because of an oversight by the English astronomer Francis Baily in the 19th century.
oggetti/leone-minore/stelle/0/significat: From the Latin for 'the principal one': even without the letter Alpha it is the brightest. An orange giant.
oggetti/leone-minore/stelle/1/significat: Second in brightness; it is a system of two stars very close together.
oggetti/lepre/cosa: A small constellation below Orion's feet: a quadrilateral of stars that looks like a crouching hare.
oggetti/lepre/quando: Evenings from December to February, highest in January at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/lepre/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon, just below Rigel and Orion. From the southern hemisphere it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/lepre/come: With the naked eye; with binoculars, look for the globular cluster M79, a small smudge in the southern part of the constellation.
oggetti/lepre/origine: Lepus is Latin for 'hare'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/lepre/storia: In the sky the hare is chased by Orion and his hunting dogs, Canis Major and Canis Minor. Here you find R Leporis, known as 'Hind's Crimson Star', one of the reddest stars in the sky.
oggetti/lepre/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the hare'. It is a yellowish-white supergiant, very far away.
oggetti/lepre/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the camels quenching their thirst'.
oggetti/lepre/stelle/2/significato: An orange giant, the third brightest.
oggetti/bilancia/cosa: A zodiac constellation between Virgo and Scorpius: a quadrilateral of modest stars.
oggetti/bilancia/quando: Evenings from May to July, highest in June at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/bilancia/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon, west (to the right) of Antares and the head of Scorpius. From the southern hemisphere it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/bilancia/come: With the naked eye; through binoculars Zubenelgenubi (α Lib) appears as a pair of stars.
oggetti/bilancia/origine: Libra is Latin for 'scales'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD), although he called it 'the Claws' of Scorpius; it was the Romans who turned it into a pair of scales.
oggetti/bilancia/storia: It is the only sign of the zodiac that represents an object rather than a living being. It is often linked to Astraea, goddess of justice, who is pictured in nearby Virgo.
oggetti/bilancia/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic for 'the northern claw' (of the scorpion): a reminder of when these stars were the claws of Scorpius.
oggetti/bilancia/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the southern claw'. Through binoculars it appears double.
oggetti/bilancia/stelle/2/significato: From the Latin 'brachium', 'arm'. It is a red giant.
oggetti/lupo/cosa: A southern constellation between Scorpius and Centaurus: a dense group of moderately bright stars.
oggetti/lupo/quando: Evenings from May to July, highest in June at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/lupo/dove: From central Italy only its northern part can be seen, skimming the southern horizon, west of Scorpius; from Sicily and southern Italy the main stars also appear, but very low. From the southern hemisphere it is high, almost overhead.
oggetti/lupo/come: With the naked eye, under a dark sky and with a clear southern horizon; from Italy it has no easy objects.
oggetti/lupo/origine: Lupus is Latin for 'wolf'. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD); the Greeks simply called it 'the wild beast'.
oggetti/lupo/storia: For the Greeks it was just some animal, speared by the lance of nearby Centaurus; the name wolf caught on with the Romans. In the year 1006 the brightest supernova in recorded history appeared here, observed in China, Egypt and Europe.
oggetti/lupo/stelle/0/significato: A hot blue-white star, the brightest in Lupus.
oggetti/lupo/stelle/1/significato: Also blue-white, like many stars in this area.
oggetti/lupo/stelle/2/significato: Blue-white: together with Men and KeKouan it belongs to a large group of young stars stretching between Scorpius and Centaurus.
oggetti/lince/cosa: A long, faint constellation between Ursa Major and Auriga: a line of stars that is almost invisible from towns.
oggetti/lince/quando: Evenings from February to April, highest in March at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/lince/dove: From Italy it is very high, almost overhead, between Capella and the front paws of Ursa Major. From the southern hemisphere only its southern part can be seen, very low in the north.
oggetti/lince/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; it has no easy objects for binoculars.
oggetti/lince/origine: Lynx is Latin for 'lynx'. It was introduced by Johannes Hevelius in 1687.
oggetti/lince/storia: Hevelius wrote that you needed the eyes of a lynx to see it, because its stars are all faint. It has no ancient myths.
oggetti/lince/stelle/0/significato: A red giant, the only somewhat noticeable star; it lies at the southern end of the constellation.
oggetti/lince/stelle/1/significato: A double star: a telescope separates the companion.
oggetti/lince/stelle/2/significato: An orange giant, halfway along the long line of stars.
oggetti/lira/cosa: Small but very easy to find thanks to Vega, one of the brightest stars in the sky. Next to Vega there is a small parallelogram of stars.
oggetti/lira/quando: Evenings from July to September, highest in August at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/lira/dove: From Italy it is very high, almost overhead: Vega is the brightest corner of the Summer Triangle, with Deneb and Altair. From the southern hemisphere it is seen low in the north.
oggetti/lira/come: With the naked eye for Vega; through binoculars ε Lyrae appears as two stars, and through a telescope each of them splits again: it is the famous 'Double Double'.
oggetti/lira/origine: Lyra is Latin for 'lyre', the stringed instrument. It is one of Ptolemy's 48 constellations (2nd century AD).
oggetti/lira/storia: It is the lyre of Orpheus, the musician whose singing moved even the gods of the Underworld. Because of the slow movement of the Earth's axis, in about 12,000 years Vega will be close to the north celestial pole. Every April the Lyrid shooting stars seem to come from here.
oggetti/lira/stelle/0/significato: From the Arabic 'an-nasr al-waqi', 'the swooping eagle'. A white star about 25 light years away.
oggetti/lira/stelle/1/significato: From the Arabic for 'the tortoise': in myth the first lyre was made by Hermes from a tortoise shell.
oggetti/lira/stelle/2/significato: An Arabic name linked to the lyre. It is two stars that eclipse each other: the light changes over about 13 days.
oggetti/mensa/cosa: The faintest constellation in the whole sky: none of its stars reaches magnitude 5. It lies near the south celestial pole, below the Large Magellanic Cloud.
oggetti/mensa/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere at 34° south it never sets, and the best evenings are from December to February, highest in January at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/mensa/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it is towards the south, halfway up the sky, just below the Large Magellanic Cloud, which partly spills over its borders.
oggetti/mensa/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns; the finest sight is the edge of the Large Magellanic Cloud, visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/mensa/origine: Mensa is Latin for 'table'. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 as Mons Mensae, 'Table Mountain'.
oggetti/mensa/storia: It commemorates Table Mountain, the flat-topped mountain above Cape Town, where Lacaille observed the southern sky. It is the only constellation dedicated to a place on Earth; it is said that Lacaille put it below the Large Magellanic Cloud because the mountain is often covered by a cloud.
oggetti/mensa/stelle/0/significato: A star similar to the Sun about 33 light years away: even though it is close, it is barely visible to the naked eye.
oggetti/mensa/stelle/1/significato: Second in brightness; you need a very dark sky.
oggetti/microscopio/cosa: A small southern constellation of faint stars, below Capricornus.
oggetti/microscopio/quando: Evenings from August to October, highest in September at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/microscopio/dove: From Italy it is low on the southern horizon, below Capricornus. From the southern hemisphere it passes almost overhead.
oggetti/microscopio/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky, far from towns, and a clear southern horizon.
oggetti/microscopio/origine: Microscopium is Latin for 'microscope'. It was introduced by Lacaille in 1751-52.
oggetti/microscopio/storia: Lacaille wanted to pay tribute to the scientific instruments of his day: the microscope had opened up the discovery of the world of the infinitely small.
oggetti/microscopio/stelle/0/significato: The brightest, even though it carries the letter Gamma: it is a yellow giant.
oggetti/microscopio/stelle/1/significato: A white star, almost as bright as Gamma.
oggetti/microscopio/stelle/2/significato: Despite the letter Alpha, it is only the fourth brightest.
oggetti/unicorno/cosa: A faint constellation in the middle of the Winter Triangle, formed by Betelgeuse, Sirius and Procyon. The winter Milky Way runs through it.
oggetti/unicorno/quando: Evenings from January to March, highest in February at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/unicorno/dove: From Italy it is halfway up the sky towards the south, east of Orion, inside the Winter Triangle. From the southern hemisphere it is seen high in the north.
oggetti/unicorno/come: You need a dark sky; with binoculars, look for the open cluster M50, between Sirius and Procyon.
oggetti/unicorno/origine: Monoceros is the Greek name for the unicorn. It was introduced by Plancius in 1612-13: it is not one of the ancient constellations.
oggetti/unicorno/storia: The unicorn was an animal of legends and medieval bestiaries, believed to be real for centuries. Plancius used faint stars that did not belong to any of Ptolemy's figures. The Rosette Nebula, famous in photographs, is found here.
oggetti/unicorno/stelle/0/significato: The brightest: through a telescope it splits into three blue-white stars, one of the most beautiful triple stars in the sky.
oggetti/unicorno/stelle/1/significato: An orange giant, second in brightness.
oggetti/mosca/cosa: A small southern constellation just below the Southern Cross: a few fairly bright stars gathered in a compact group.
oggetti/mosca/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere at 34° south it never sets, and the best evenings are from April to June, highest in May at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/mosca/dove: From Italy it never rises. From the southern hemisphere it is high in the south, just below the Southern Cross, on the side towards the pole.
oggetti/mosca/come: With the naked eye; next to it is the Coalsack, a dark nebula that looks like a black patch in the Milky Way near the Southern Cross.
oggetti/mosca/origine: Musca is Latin for 'fly'. It began as Apis, 'the bee', introduced by Plancius at the end of the 16th century from the observations of Keyser and de Houtman; the name Musca caught on in the 18th century with Lacaille.
oggetti/mosca/storia: For a time it was called Musca Australis, 'the southern fly', to distinguish it from a northern Fly near Aries, which has since been abolished.
oggetti/mosca/stelle/0/significato: A hot blue-white star, the brightest in the constellation.
oggetti/mosca/stelle/1/significato: It is two blue-white stars very close together, which can only be separated with a telescope.
oggetti/squadra/cosa: A small southern constellation between Scorpius and Centaurus, set in the Milky Way, with no obvious shape.
oggetti/squadra/quando: It cannot be seen from Italy; from the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from June to August, highest in July at around 9-10 pm.
oggetti/squadra/dove: From central Italy it never rises; from Sicily and southern Italy you can glimpse part of it, skimming the horizon. From the southern hemisphere it is high, almost overhead, next to the tail of Scorpius.
oggetti/squadra/come: A faint constellation: you need a dark sky; with binoculars, look for the open cluster NGC 6087, among rich star fields of the Milky Way.
oggetti/squadra/origine: Norma is Latin for 'set square', the drawing tool. Lacaille introduced it in 1751-52 as Norma et Regula, 'set square and ruler'.
oggetti/squadra/storia: Lacaille dedicated it to the tools of draughtsmen and builders. The stars he called Alpha and Beta are now part of Scorpius, because the borders have changed: that is why the brightest is Gamma.
oggetti/squadra/stelle/0/significato: A yellow giant, the brightest star in the constellation.
oggetti/squadra/stelle/1/significato: A double star, second in brightness.
